questions.prompt: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg trolley. What is its acceleration?
What resultant force gives a 1200 kg car an acceleration of 2.5 m/s²?
A force of 20 N gives an object an acceleration of 4 m/s². What is its mass?
The mass of a trolley is doubled but the resultant force stays the same. What happens to the acceleration?
questions.explain: a = F ÷ m: doubling m halves a.

options: The mass of a small apple
The force needed to move 1 kg by 1 m
The force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
The weight of 1 kg on Earth

feedback.3: The weight of 1 kg is about 9.8 N.

questions.prompt: A 50 kg student stands on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). What is the student’s weight?
A 2 kg box is pushed with 18 N; friction is 6 N. What is its acceleration?
In a trolley experiment, the graph of acceleration against force (constant mass) is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
options: Acceleration is inversely proportional to force
questions.explain: A straight line through the origin means direct proportion: a ∝ F.

questions.prompt: Explain, using F = ma, why a loaded lorry needs a much longer distance to stop than a car with the same brakes.
questions.modelAnswer: The lorry has a much bigger mass. With a similar braking force, a = F ÷ m is much smaller, so the lorry decelerates more slowly. At a smaller deceleration it takes longer, and further, to reduce its speed to zero.
rubric: Same force gives smaller deceleration (a = F/m)
Smaller deceleration means longer stopping distance
questions.explain: Criterion D: applying physics to road safety.
